$comment: The state transitions of one item (a ticket) through the human pipeline, as the code and prompts implement them today. Each transition names the ACTOR that causes it, the SKILL that does the work, the MARKER that records it, and WHERE it is implemented. Topology is name/src/dst only; every other field is annotation.
item: a ticket, from filing to merged

actors.user: a person, via a board gesture (drag, button) or a CLI command
actors.daemon: the host process — it launches agents, posts their started markers, and is the only thing with push credentials
actors.skill: an agent running in a container, following the named prompt

unclassified_markers.doc: Posted by the pipeline but deliberately not transitions: they record content or decorate the card, and the item's state is unchanged by them.

dual_role.plan: A transition inside a self-planning fix run (fix-plan-written: fix-planning to fixing, the run writing the plan it is about to carry out) and a record of content everywhere else, where a planner attaches a plan to a ticket that does not move until [human:plan-ready]. Measured on the 59-history corpus: dropping it from this list turns 21 histories' plan markers into refusals, 16 of them at `filed` or `planning` where nothing moved. The overlap is what keeps those 16 from being reported as defects.
dual_role.bug-verdict: A transition out of triaging — to fix-planning on a confirmed bug, to challenging on a not-a-bug, which is why the corpus records bug-verdict@preflight as a known ambiguity rather than a defect — and a record of content when it lands anywhere else. Dropping it from this list adds 2 refusals at `implementing`.

states.name: filed
states.doc: The ticket exists. No pipeline activity.
states.holds: The ticket is open and carries no pipeline marker.
states.stale_when: Never. Waiting is what Backlog is for, and an item may rest here indefinitely.
states.if_nothing_happens: Nothing, with one named exception. The machine starts no pipeline STAGE nobody asked for: a person may hand a Backlog ticket straight to an agent — a directly invoked plan or ticket-review run posts its markers here without the board dispatching anything — but no stage begins on its own. The exception is the idea drafter (actor: daemon): capturing an idea IS the ask for a draft, so the daemon launches `idea-draft-<KEY>` on capture and, debounced, on a tracker-side TITLE change (the title is the input a draft is made from; arming on any UpdatedAt advance would relaunch the run the drafter's own write caused) — where: `cmd/cmddaemon.ideaDraftLauncherFunc` and `internal/daemon.IdeaDraftWatcher.Observe`. It writes the ticket's description and posts [human:idea-draft-started] / [human:idea-draft]; when the run dies without producing a draft the DAEMON posts [human:idea-draft-failed] in its place (a run that dies on its first API call never gets a turn in which to report) — where: `internal/daemon.RunAuxFailureWatch`. The drafter is ALSO launched by a person (actor: user), from the Product-Backlog card menu's "Recreate description": the same producer, the same agent name, one flag that bypasses the overwrite guard for that one call — where: `internal/daemon.Server.handleRecreateDescription`, `cmd/cmddaemon.ideaDraftLauncherFunc` and `internal/ideadraft.VerdictFor`. It posts the same three markers. None of them is a transition; the item does not move and no stage runs.

states.name: ticket-review
states.doc: The pre-planning gate is judging whether solving this ticket solves the problem.
states.holds: The pre-planning gate is running as the FIRST PHASE of the planning dispatch, so the agent that owns it is registered under the planning stage, not this one.
states.stale_when: Past StuckRunningGrace with no live agent, like any running stage.
states.if_nothing_happens: The agent's death is recorded as a PLANNING failure, because planning is the stage it runs under. Note the gap: the backlog stage has no *-failed marker of its own (failedTypeFor returns none for it), so neither the live watcher nor the durable pass can red a card derived at backlog/running directly — recovery here depends entirely on the enclosing planning dispatch.

states.name: ticket-reviewed
states.doc: The gate returned a verdict: ready, reframed, superseded, escalated or rejected. The last three are stop decisions.
states.holds: A verdict is recorded with one of five heads.
states.stale_when: Never — a verdict is a resting point, not work in progress.
states.if_nothing_happens: For `ready` and `reframed`, the same run continues into planning without anything further. For the three stop heads the item rests in Backlog with the reason on the ticket; only a person restarts it.

states.name: planning
states.doc: A planner is exploring the codebase and writing an implementation plan.
states.holds: A planner owns the stage and [human:planning-started] is the item's newest planning marker.
states.note: One exception to the recovery rule: a run that attached its plan before dying is not redded. Both the live exit watcher and the durable pass post the handoff on its behalf and the item moves to planned (plan-handoff-completed). It applies only where the plan is on the TICKET — in split topology the plan is an engineering ticket the daemon never saw created, so nothing here can complete it.

states.name: planned
states.doc: A plan is attached to the ticket. The item waits for a human to start the build.
states.holds: A [human:plan] comment is attached and no build has started.
states.stale_when: Never. A plan nobody has acted on is not a fault.
states.if_nothing_happens: Nothing. The machine does not begin an implementation on its own — a plan waits for a person to start the build.

states.name: nothing-to-do
states.doc: The planning stage ended with nothing to plan, and the marker's required reason says why: merged (the planner proved the work is already on the base), duplicate (the ticket-review gate found another ticket carries it), escalated (the gate created a design ticket that has to be decided first) or rejected (not a real problem). Clean terminal; the board labels each reason on its own and renders only merged as shipped (SC-5326).
states.holds: A [human:nothing-to-do] marker with evidence and a reason from the closed set merged|duplicate|escalated|rejected is the newest planning-stage marker. Clean terminal.
states.if_nothing_happens: Nothing. The machine must never re-run its own clean terminal, which is exactly why reopen is a separate entry point from every retry gesture: the automatic relaunch drives the identical same-stage request.

states.name: preflight
states.doc: The fix run is resolving what it may do and settling what the evidence can settle, before any work.
states.holds: A fix run owns the implementation stage and is resolving what it may do before any work.

states.name: triaging
states.doc: The run is reproducing the report to reach a verdict.
states.holds: The run is reproducing the report; the implementation stage is claimed.

states.name: challenging
states.doc: A skeptic is trying to refute a not-a-bug or undetermined verdict before it is acted on.
states.holds: A skeptic is trying to refute a not-a-bug or undetermined verdict. It runs ONCE — a verdict that survives is not re-challenged.

states.name: resolved-no-fix
states.doc: The no-fix verdict survived the challenge. Clean terminal — the ticket needs no code change.
states.holds: The no-fix verdict survived the challenge. Clean terminal — no code change is warranted.
states.if_nothing_happens: Nothing. As with nothing-to-do, only an explicitly human call may re-run a clean terminal.

states.name: fix-planning
states.doc: The self-planning fix run is producing its own plan.
states.holds: The self-planning fix run is writing its own plan, because it entered from a report rather than from a planned ticket.

states.name: fixing
states.doc: A regression test that fails first, then the change that makes it pass.
states.holds: A regression test that fails first exists, or is being written, along with the change that makes it pass.

states.name: verifying
states.doc: Proving the test fails before and passes after, on a green suite.
states.holds: The fix exists and its fails-before/passes-after evidence is being produced by something other than the code that wrote it.
states.note: This is the state SC-1136 froze in: a NOT DONE verify that halted silently left a card reading "being fixed" forever, which is the dead end the durable pass exists to close.

states.name: implementing
states.doc: A plan executor is carrying out an attached plan (the non-bug path).
states.holds: A plan executor is carrying out an ATTACHED plan. A launch onto a ticket with no plan is refused before any agent claims the stage.

states.name: handed-off
states.doc: Branch and commits are recorded on the ticket, checked reachable. A person may also ship it straight from the command line (`human deploy`), which is the one non-daemon move that leaves this state.
states.holds: Branch and commits are recorded on the ticket AND the commits were verified reachable on the branch before the marker was posted. A verdict recorded BEFORE this handoff no longer governs the item when the handoff names a commit that verdict did not judge; a handoff naming only judged commits records what the branch holds and leaves the verdict standing (SC-5475). The handoff also says WHO reviews it: a `review: inline` line means the run that posted it is the reviewer and owns the verification stage from this moment, before any `[human:review-started]` exists; its absence means the daemon must chain one.
states.stale_when: The review was never chained — the live hook was lost to a daemon restart.
states.if_nothing_happens: reconcileOrphanedHandoffs chains the review for a handoff newer than the newest verification marker that names a commit the verdict did not judge, but only when the commits are DEFINITELY present on this machine. A clean absence or an unreadable check leaves the card alone rather than redding work another machine may be able to serve. A `review: inline` handoff is left alone while the `board-<key>-implementation` container that posted it is alive on this machine (liveStageAgent), and chained the moment it is not — or, where liveness cannot be established, once StuckRunningGrace has passed. Without that bound this state would trade a double review for a card nobody ever reviews (SC-430 again).

states.name: in-review
states.doc: A reviewer is checking the change against the ticket's acceptance criteria. In a board fix run this happens inline, in the same warm container.
states.holds: A reviewer owns the verification stage and is checking the change against the ticket's acceptance criteria.

states.name: reviewed
states.doc: The review returned a verdict. A failing verdict blocks the deploy and sends the item back to be rebuilt.
states.holds: A verdict is recorded, and it judges the round the item was in when it was posted. The board reads the daemon's blocking DECISION, never the verdict string. A verdict is not evidence that the run which produced it has ended: since SC-782 the review runs INLINE in the implementation container, so `[human:review-complete]` is posted from a container that is still alive and still holding the bind-mounted checkout, minutes before it exits (measured on SC-5592: verdict 10:12Z, container gone ~10:24Z).
states.stale_when: A [human:ready-for-review] handoff, newer than the verdict, naming a commit the verdict did not judge. The verdict judged the round it was posted against and records which commits that was (review-complete's optional commits field), so the question is about the work, not the clock: a rebuild handed back awaits a fresh review, while a handoff re-posted to record the reviewer's own commit is not a new round and stales nothing (SC-5475).
states.if_nothing_happens: A passing verdict waits for the Deploy gesture, and the gesture then waits for the checkout: the done stage does not push, freshen or open a pull request while the implementation container (or the verification container) is still alive on the machine that runs it. It polls every 15s for up to DeployCheckoutWaitBound (15m) and then abandons the launch, recording nothing (deploy-launch-deferred) — an implementation container still alive that long after its verdict is hung, and the stuck-running sweep answers for it rather than the deploy redding the wrong stage (SC-5691). A rework hands off again, and that handoff leaves this state: chainReviewAfterCleanBuild launches the review live, and reconcileOrphanedHandoffs recovers it when the live hook is lost. The daemon also acts here on the legacy PR path.

states.name: deploying
states.doc: The daemon pushed the branch and opened a draft pull request.
states.holds: A deploy is under way and recorded on the ticket. One engine run holds the process-wide deploy gate, so no second deploy for any card runs beside it, and no deploy for THIS card was allowed to start while its own implementation container still held the checkout (SC-5691). On the board's PR-loop entry the branch is pushed and a DRAFT pull request is open; on the `human deploy` entry the marker is posted first and the push follows — and since F10 that push also opens the pull request in DRAFT and hands it to the machine reviewer (pr-opened), unless a still-current approval already names the exact head being shipped (approval-reused) or the person passed --ready (deploy-skips-review). The start marker carries an `override:` line for every guard the deploy walked past, so a merge that skipped the review says so on the ticket.
states.stale_when: Past deployTimeout + StuckRunningGrace (60 minutes) — not the ordinary 15 — measured from the moment the ENGINE's clock started, not from the marker post. A deploy reports no agent liveness at all and its CI gate legitimately blocks for the whole of deployTimeout, so the stuck-running sweep gives it its own grace (stuckPastGrace, internal/daemon/board_reconcile.go); judging it by the ordinary rule reds a healthy deploy and relaunches a second one on top of it. The engine's clock is the instant it left the unbounded deployGate; while it is still queued, the clock is the last time the queue moved, so a deploy waiting its turn is spared while the queue advances and judged once it has stopped. On a machine that is not running the deploy — a peer daemon, or one that restarted and lost the record — the marker clock is used instead, so the sweep is bounded rather than blind.

states.name: pr-review
states.doc: The machine reviewer is reading the open pull request.
states.holds: The machine reviewer is reading the open pull request; the newest done-stage marker is a loop-started marker.

states.name: pr-fix
states.doc: The machine fixer is addressing the review's findings on the local branch.
states.holds: The machine fixer is committing to the LOCAL branch and never pushing, so the reviewer reads the new commit rather than a stale pushed head.

states.name: ci-gate
states.doc: Every check must be green before the merge.
states.holds: The review converged and every check must be green before the merge. A head that reports no checks at all is not green: it is pending until DeployNoChecksGrace has elapsed, because a freshly pushed head (a freshness rebase, a deploy-fixer push) has none for the minute or two its CI takes to register, and only past the grace does absence mean a repository without CI. If the base moved on, the branch is rebased and CI re-gated on the new head first. The re-gate after a freshness rebase is bound to the commit the rebase PUBLISHED: while the forge still reports a different head on the pull request, there is no verdict to read — never passing, never failing — because the checks it would answer with belong to the tip that was just replaced (SC-5395). Past DeployHeadWaitTimeout the gate stops rather than reading them, and that stop is not a code failure, so it never dispatches a fixer. A red head is not automatically a broken build either: the gate splits the failing checks by whether a code change could turn them green, and a head red ONLY on checks no code change can turn green — a contributor-signature job, a bot comment step — is waited out for DeployExternalCheckGrace the way an absence is, because such a check routinely re-runs. Past that grace the gate stops with those checks named and a re-run remedy, and that stop is not a code failure, so it dispatches no fixer. The aggregate reds on the first failing check without waiting for the others to answer, so a check a code change could still turn green — one still ChecksPending, a build or a test not yet concluded — keeps the head from being judged external-only at all, however long that grace has run; only once every OTHER check has concluded does the grace, and then the stop, apply (SC-5843 r1). A failing check the gate cannot attribute — an unreadable per-check read, a name and origin it does not know — stays code-fixable, so no carve-out can silence a real build break (SC-5843).

states.name: deploy-fixing
states.doc: A CI failure, a rebase conflict at the gate, or a base merge that conflicted before a review round dispatched the deploy fixer instead of failing the item; a fixer sent before the review hands back to the reviewer on done (the deploy-fix-started marker's `before: review` field), the gate's fixer re-runs the deploy.
states.holds: A mechanical failure — red CI or a rebase conflict — dispatched the fixer instead of failing the item. The fixer's container holds no push credentials.
states.note: Rounds are separately bounded by DefaultDeployFixRounds (2); past that the escalation names the condition that is blocking rather than advising a retry that would hit the same wall. Its agent is board-<key>-deployfix and the 15-minute grace applies to it: the deploy engine's own 60-minute clock does not cover a running fixer, because DeployBranch unregisters its run (deployRunFinished) as soon as it dispatches one. What spares a working fixer is the liveness join, not the grace. The same join spares it from the PR-loop re-drive: where the fixer's own deploy-fix-started post was refused, the thread stays frozen at the loop's marker and the card still reads mid-loop, so reconcilePRLoops asks all three done-stage names rather than the two halves (SC-5591). A round that ends in an outage is not charged: deployFixRounds refunds a deploy-fix-started marker followed by a deploy-outage one, so the bound counts fixer rounds that actually ran (SC-5592). The bound is per ticket but not per ticket's life: a person's Retry deploy on the card mints a [human:deploy-retry] grant worth one further round, counted by deployFixGrants and spent by the deploy-fix-started marker that carries grant: retry — so a card whose two rounds are spent is asked about rather than stuck, and the machine's own re-drives (ApplyRetryTransition) mint nothing (SC-5595).

states.name: merged
states.doc: Merged, branch deleted, ticket closed. The shipping terminal.
states.holds: Merged, branch deleted, ticket closed. Past the merge, cleanup and closing are best-effort and never fail the item.
states.if_nothing_happens: Nothing. This is the shipping terminal — the only state with no actor able to leave it.

states.name: awaiting-decision
states.doc: The item is parked on a genuine fork. Only a human choosing an answer moves it.

board.note: Idle in whatever column the card was in, with an open [human:options] block — pauseOnOpenOptions turns running or failed into idle. "Decision needed" is not a BoardState; the open block is what distinguishes it.

states.holds: An open [human:options] block names this item's own stage, or an earlier stage the answer would rework.
states.stale_when: Never by time. A pause on an open decision is deliberate, and BOTH the live guard (stagePausedOnOptions) and the reconcile pass exclude it from the stuck-running sweep on purpose — a card waiting for a person is not a card that has hung.
states.if_nothing_happens: Nothing. This is the one state the machine may not resolve for itself, which is the whole point of raising a fork rather than guessing.

states.name: queued
states.doc: A decision is answered and names a stage to run; nothing has started it yet.

board.note: Only the three stages an options block may relaunch — planning, implementation, verification (optionStages) — so backlog and done never carry it. Synthesized by optionChosenQueued when [human:option-chosen] is the newest board-relevant signal; any classified marker newer than the choice supersedes it.

states.holds: The newest board-relevant marker is an [human:option-chosen] whose block names a resumable stage, and that stage's started marker has not been posted. TWO different situations hold here and the record tells them apart: an ordinary answer is queued for a launch that is on its way, while an answer carrying a `waits-for` field is HELD — it named a ticket that goes first, and the stage must not start until that ticket is done.
states.stale_when: Past QueuedLaunchGrace (2m) with no live agent for the stage. Recording the choice and launching the stage are the two halves of one ApplyOption call, in that order, so the ordinary window is microseconds; the grace exists only so a reconcile tick landing inside it does not race a launch already on its way. A HELD card is never stale by time: it is doing exactly what a person told it to, for as long as the ticket it waits for takes.
states.if_nothing_happens: reconcileQueuedLaunch starts the stage the decision named, on the next tick past the grace — unless the answer was a sequencing one, in which case that same pass HOLDS the card and starts it on the first tick after the ticket it named is done or closed. A held card whose blocker cannot be read stays held: starting the work is the one outcome the person's answer ruled out, and a deliberate wait has no time bound to give up at, so the way out of an unreadable one is a person dropping the card on its own column. Otherwise it relaunches through the CHARGED, capped path (DefaultStageRetries), so a stage that cannot be launched is tried twice and then left for a person rather than forever — and a refusal that starts nothing, the plan gate, is not charged at all and routes the card itself to needs-planning; a hold is charged nothing either, because nothing was attempted. A single-flight refusal — an agent already running the stage on this machine — is charged nothing either, and posts no started marker, so the card simply stays queued for the next tick (SC-4244). It deliberately does not go through the ordinary retry classifier: that reads the stage's last recorded exit, which here is the ExitNeedsInput of the stage that RAISED the decision, and would classify the card as one to leave for a human — refusing to start exactly the cards this pass exists for. Until SC-3865 nothing watched this state at all: it exists so the stuck-running sweep will not red a card whose decision was just answered (SC-1320), and it achieved that by being a state no sweep looked at — one property, protection from one side and a hole from the other. The pass could not in fact start anything until the transition that admits a queued card existed: every re-drive was rejected as a non-advance by the forward-only rule and charged for the refusal. Two held cards waiting for each other stay held: the release pass names the pair in the log and the board reports it on both cards, and the way out is a person starting one of them.

states.name: stopped
states.doc: A stage gave up and said why: a spent budget, an unreviewable change, a failed deploy. Needs a human.
states.holds: A stage gave up and the marker says why, naming the blocking condition rather than offering a gesture that cannot work. Landing here TWICE with no relaunch in between is absorbed rather than re-told: stageAlreadyFailed (SC-3857) reads the stage's own newest marker and suppresses only a repeat POST of the identical *-failed marker, so a second, unrelated exit event for the same dead run does not re-date an hour-old corpse as freshly broken. The exception is a genuine second failure AFTER a relaunch — every relaunch that actually started an agent posts the stage's own *-started marker before the agent that follows it can exit, so a *-started marker newer than the failure flips the guard back off and the new failure posts and re-dates as it always did. A relaunch REFUSED because an agent is already running on this machine posts nothing and leaves the guard on — see stage-relaunch-refused (SC-4244). Suppressing the post does NOT suppress the automatic in-place relaunch below: the ordinary ending IS a skill posting its own *-failed marker and recording its own stage outcome before it exits, so the marker this ending posted is already the stage's newest by the time the exit event is processed — indistinguishable from a stale duplicate by marker history alone. The relaunch is decided from the stage's own recorded exit class instead, independent of the marker thread, so a genuine retryable ending still gets its bounded relaunch even though its own marker cannot be re-posted (revised after a second-opinion probe showed the first cut of this guard silently dropped that relaunch for the everyday retryable-review path, not only the rare unrecorded-exit corner). The needs-person and silence-reap endings are the exception: each decides its post and its relaunch (or lack of one) in a single synchronous step the daemon itself performs, so an already-failed marker there can only be a fully-completed EARLIER cycle, and both the post and the relaunch stay suppressed for those two. The stop is about ONE stage, and the card is not: a card carries the newest marker of the whole item, so a failure recorded in one stage takes a card whose OTHER stage is still running, and the red then asks a person to intervene on work that is still being done (measured on SC-3853, where a done-stage failure sat over a live implementation agent until that agent's own relaunch turned the card green again). The board answers it by joining the other stage's container before it renders the failure as the last word — a card carrying BoardCard.RunningStage reads as work in progress while an agent is found, and reds exactly as before when none is (SC-4406). A stop an agent chose (`needs-human-work`) carries its evidence: the marker's `kind`, `evidence`, `attempted` and `release` fields, mirrored as a `blocker` object in the stage record (shared/exit-contract.md, SC-5179). The exit name alone is not evidence that the stop was necessary; a stop without the four is an unexplained stop, and a person reading the card later has only the marker and the stage record to judge whether it was. One such stop is the machine's own and not an agent's: a host this daemon's proxy refused by policy, redded from an outage-shaped ending with kind unavailable-dependency and the proxy.domains line as its release (egress-blocked-by-policy-*, SC-5840).
states.stale_when: Never automatically — a stop is a request for a person.
states.if_nothing_happens: Not nothing — this is the state most easily mistaken for a dead end. Within DefaultStageRetries (2) the machine relaunches the failed stage IN PLACE: the failure is recorded first and the relaunch is the same transition a person Retry gesture issues, so every existing guard applies unchanged. Past the budget it waits for a person. Three further cases are the done stage's own recovery. Two are in reconcileShippedFailures (internal/daemon/board_reconcile.go), which RE-READS the pull request rather than trusting the single observation that reddened the card: a done-stage failure whose pull request the forge reports MERGED is retired with a [human:deployed] marker, because the work shipped out of band and the red is stale rather than true; and a done-stage failure whose pull request is not merged but is DEFINITELY SHIPPABLE — the forge reports it mergeable and every check it reports has passed — is re-driven instead (redeploy-when-shippable): the pass issues the same in-place done-stage retry the Retry deploy gesture issues, so a pull request that turned green a minute after the red no longer sits behind a red card until a person notices (SC-3640). Neither arm fires on an unknown state — a probe that errors, a check still pending, or a head reporting no checks at all leaves the card exactly as it is. The re-drive additionally requires the newest done-stage marker to be the deploy failure (a pr-review-failed card is a verdict about content, which green CI does not answer), no live done-stage agent and no deploy running in this process, a branch this machine can resolve, and FailedRecoveryGrace (5m) since the failure; its attempts on one pull request HEAD back off from 2m to 30m, so a re-drive that starts but does not merge — which posts its own fresh deploy-failed — does not reset the pacing, and only a head that has genuinely moved earns a fresh attempt. It has deliberately NO upper bound in time — a card left red overnight is the case it exists to clear — and charges no stage-retry attempt, because it acts on positive evidence that the deploy is ready rather than on a guess that another attempt might work. The third is shipped-after-stop: a deploy that was still running when the failure was posted over it — a deploy fixer that converged after a spurious [human:deploy-failed], or a re-drop onto a branch already in the base — records its own merge with the same [human:deployed] marker rather than leaving the stale failure standing. A record that cannot be posted is logged and the ticket is left OPEN rather than closed, so the card stays visible and the next pass can repair it: a Done status over a failed-deploy trail is the one outcome this state must never produce (SC-5594). Accounting rules keep that relaunch honest (SC-5104): a needs-input exit is a person's only while an open, unanswered [human:options] block stands on the ticket — without one it is an empty claim and takes the same bounded relaunch, redding past the budget with the attempts on record; an attempt is charged only for a relaunch that actually started an agent, so an errored launch that started nothing refunds and one that started but lost its started marker stays charged; and a failure for a stage the card has already moved past (the review verdict and PR loop posted after a verification failure, SC-3853) is retired uncharged, because there is nothing left to relaunch. The live relaunch happens at the moment the exit is processed; when that moment is lost — a restart between the failure and its handling, a failed comment read, a launch that errored before anything started — reconcileFailedStages (internal/daemon/board_reconcile_failed.go) revisits the card: from FailedRecoveryGrace (5m) after the failure, so the live path acts first, until FailedRecoveryBound (6h) after it, so a failure nobody could recover is left to a person; it runs the same StageRetry policy, so the budget, the needs-input rule and the stale-failure rule all apply, and its attempts on one stage back off from 2m to 30m so a persistent launch error costs a handful of tries rather than one per tick. It leaves alone a done-stage failure (the deploy's own recovery above owns it: the merged probe, the shippable re-drive and the deploy fixer), a live agent, an open decision, a silence-reap give-up, an egress-blocked give-up (egress-blocked-by-policy-*, SC-5840 — a policy denial does not clear on its own, so this marker is never re-driven by age alone; the release is a person's own Retry after the config edit) and a standing plan-stuck escalation; the retry policy itself declines a deliberate needs-human-work stop. Past FailedRecoveryBound it posts nothing — the standing *-failed marker and the attempts on record are the trail, the daemon logs the bound once per stage, and `human fsm where` names it; a give-up marker there carried the failure reason into a body the sentinel scanners read and collided with the silence-reap sentinels (SC-5170).

states.name: substrate-down
states.doc: A stage reported the thing it needs was unreachable. Not a failure — it spends no retry budget and is relaunched when the substrate returns.
states.holds: A stage reported the thing it needs was unreachable. Nothing about the work is wrong, so it spends no retry budget. And the thing that was unreachable must be a substrate, not this host's own policy: a host the daemon's proxy refused never enters here (egress-blocked-by-policy-*), because the wait this state grants would be a wait for a config edit nobody has been asked to make.
states.stale_when: The outage has lasted past OutageWaitBound (6 hours). An outage that never ends looks exactly like one that will return, until someone measures how long it has run.
states.if_nothing_happens: Each reconcile tick relaunches the stage WITHOUT charging DefaultStageRetries, until the substrate returns and a *-started marker supersedes the outage. Past OutageWaitBound the card is handed to a person instead — still charging nothing. The relaunch still meets the launch gate, and one substrate the gate now judges is the model API itself: a host whose proxy policy blocks it fails the `egress` doctor check and starts nothing at all, so the card waits in place rather than re-driving a stage that can only report the same outage (SC-4819). See not_states / `a host that cannot launch`. A card already standing here when the daemon learned the difference is converted rather than re-driven: reconcileOutage asks the same block question each tick and, on a standing refusal, reds the card once with the host and the config line and stops (SC-5840).

events.name: start-ticket-review
events.where: cmd/cmdplan — /human-ticket-review invoked directly against a Backlog ticket
events.doc: The pre-planning gate, run on its own: before any code is planned, something asks whether solving this ticket solves the problem.
events.prompt: human-ticket-reviewer-agent.md — the gate posts its own ticket-review-started marker

events.name: ticket-review-verdict
events.doc: The gate returned one of five heads. `ready` and `reframed` continue into planning; `superseded`, `escalated` and `rejected` are stop decisions and say why, so the item rests in Backlog with the reason on the ticket rather than quietly never being picked up.

events.name: start-planning
events.where: board_transition.go launchPlanningOrFix, from launchForwardStage / isPlanningRetry / launchDecidedStage
events.guard: the ticket belongs to no fix pipeline: classifyFixPipeline returns fixNone from the recorded [human:pipeline] marker, the ticket kind and the marker heuristic, in that order (SC-5793)
events.doc: A drop on Planning. From planned it is a replan; from stopped or substrate-down it is a retry in place. Every one of these dispatches classifies first: planning is the stage for tickets whose plan a planner writes, so a bug or security ticket takes fix-resumed-instead-of-planning to preflight instead — the same question the rework and build-retry paths ask (SC-2986/SC-2989), asked at the planning sites too (SC-5793).

events.name: plan-attached
events.doc: The plan itself is attached as a [human:plan] comment; plan-ready is what moves the item. Planning run on its own attaches a plan to a ticket the board never dispatched, so the marker arrives with no planning-started before it.
events.where: internal/claude/embed/human-plan-skill.md posts plan-ready as its last step, whether or not the board dispatched it

events.name: plan-handoff-completed
events.where: internal/daemon/board_failure.go completePlanningHandoff, from handleCleanStageEnding on the run's exit; internal/daemon/board_reconcile.go completeStrandedPlanHandoff is the durable twin for a lost exit event
events.doc: The planning handoff is two tracker writes — the plan, then plan-ready — and a run that died between them left the deliverable the next stage needs already attached. The daemon posts the handoff on the dead run's behalf rather than redding the card and re-planning an attached plan (SC-5090). Recognized by a [human:plan] comment newer than the stage's newest planning-started; the marker carries no engineering: field, so single-tracker topology only. Posting it, not merely suppressing the failure, is what moves the item: a suppressed failure leaves a card running behind a dead agent. Declines — leaving the item in `stopped` — when the stage's own newest marker is already its own planning-failed: that is a decision the run made about the ticket (the exit-contract's needs-human-work instruction), never overwritten by a handoff synthesized from the plan comment, which is also why src lists only `planning` and never `stopped`. Reached too for a silence reap (a live agent judged hung and stopped by this pass, or the zombie sweep's synthesized exit) — the body then says the run was stopped rather than exited, and the SC-2447/SC-3074 idle/budget/outstanding observation rides along as marker fields so the reap is not lost by the completion.

events.name: plan-finds-nothing-to-do
events.doc: The planner established the work is already merged (reason: merged), so there is nothing to build. A clean terminal rather than a failure — and reopenable, because it is a judgement and a person may overrule it. The ticket-review gate posts it too, with the reason its verdict maps to (superseded → duplicate, escalated → escalated, rejected → rejected): its own verdict marker classifies under the backlog stage and would leave the card reading as planning-in-progress, so a stop verdict posts the planning stage's terminal marker alongside it. The post refuses a record without a reason (SC-5326).

events.name: planning-failed
events.where: board_failure.go — guarded by stageAlreadyFailed (SC-3857): a stage already failed with no relaunch since does not re-post, but the automatic in-place relaunch still runs (deps.Retry.tryRelaunch reads the stage's own recorded exit, not the marker thread)
events.doc: The planning stage itself failed — a spent retry budget, an agent that died without a verdict. Distinct from the planner concluding there is nothing to do, which is a terminal rather than a fault and must never be reddened as one. Fires at most once per ending: a second exit event for the same dead run is absorbed (SC-3857). Also distinct from a run that died having already attached its plan, which is completed rather than reddened (plan-handoff-completed).

events.name: start-fix-run
events.where: board_transition.go ApplyFix; board_options.go launchDecidedStage → launchFixPipeline when the stage was queued by a decision
events.doc: Dropping a bug on Fix. The run is self-planning — it produces its own plan rather than requiring one. A person re-opening a [human:nothing-to-do] on a bug reaches the same dispatch: reopenResolved classifies and the fix pipeline resumes (SC-5793). A bug that already carries a plan and is dropped on Planning again lands here too: ticket kind is authoritative over plan evidence, so start-planning's guard sends it to the fix run rather than to the feature planner (SC-5793).

events.name: preflight-clear
events.doc: Preflight found no question that only a human can answer, so the run proceeds to reproduce the report. Everything the evidence could settle, it settled.

events.name: preflight-asks
events.doc: The one place the pipeline asks a question, asked up front rather than halfway through. Which of two colliding tickets goes first is not among its questions: a confirmed collision is recorded on the run and both are built, the merge gate integrating the second with the base that carries the first (SC-5274). Every preflight run is a bug or security fix, so a scope fork is not among its questions either: the ticket's Expected list is already the acceptance, and whether to do one of its items is never a question. The only fork this transition ever fires for is a person's own open work on the ticket (SC-5704).

events.name: triage-verdict-confirmed
events.doc: Triage reproduced the report, so the run continues as a confirmed bug and plans its fix. A not-a-bug or undetermined verdict goes to the skeptic instead of ending the run.

events.name: triage-verdict-no-bug
events.doc: A no-fix verdict is never acted on directly — it must survive a challenge first.

events.name: challenge-upholds
events.doc: The skeptic could not refute the not-a-bug or undetermined verdict, so it stands and the run ends without a code change. The challenge runs once — a verdict that survives it is not re-challenged. The marker is posted BEFORE the ticket is closed: it is what the board reads for the resolved column and what `reopen-fix` re-opens from, while the closed status is bookkeeping after it. The other order left a closed ticket with no record when the post was refused (SC-5839).

events.name: challenge-refutes
events.doc: The skeptic reproduced it. The run continues as a confirmed bug, using the skeptic's reproduction. Runs once — never loops back through triage.

events.name: fix-plan-written
events.doc: The self-planning fix run wrote its own plan and starts carrying it out. It plans for itself because it entered from a bug report rather than from a planned ticket, so there is no attached plan to execute.

events.name: fix-written
events.doc: A regression test that fails first, then the change that makes it pass. Verification is a separate step so the fails-before/passes-after evidence is produced by something other than the code that wrote the fix.

events.name: verify-not-done
events.guard: under the retry budget; only a failure that reproduced charges an attempt
events.doc: The verify gate found the fix wanting and the run loops back inside itself. No marker records it: [human:bug-verify] is evidence, not a transition, so nothing on the ticket distinguishes this from the fix still running. The item genuinely moves; the record does not.

events.name: fix-budget-spent
events.doc: The fix could not be made to verify within the run's budget. The item stops for a human rather than shipping a change nothing proved.

events.name: start-implementation
events.where: board_transition.go launchForwardStage / isReworkTransition / isBuildRetry / isQueuedLaunch
events.doc: The plan-executing path. From reviewed it is the rework loop — a failing review verdict sends the item back to be rebuilt with the findings. It shares its marker and four of its sources (planned, stopped, queued, substrate-down) with start-fix-run and fix-resumed-instead-of-planning, so a marker thread cannot say which move a second [human:implementation-started] recorded — only the ticket's kind can, and a replay does not have it. A write gate must therefore judge a later marker against EVERY state the history is consistent with, not the one a replay pinned: judging against the pinned branch refused the [human:no-fix-needed] record of every retried fix run (SC-5839, internal/tracker/local/pipeline.go admitMarker).

events.name: handoff-posted
events.where: posted via `human handoff post`, which verifies the commits are reachable on the branch first
events.doc: Branch and commits are recorded on the ticket for whoever reviews next. The commits are verified reachable on the branch before the marker is posted, so a handoff never names work nobody else can see. A handoff from reviewed is the rework round answering a verdict: the verdict judged the round before it, so the item is handed off again and awaits a fresh review (SC-4958). A handoff from reviewed that names only commits the verdict already judged is bookkeeping, not a round: it leaves the verdict governing and starts no review (SC-5475). The marker may also carry an optional `review:` line naming who reviews the work — `inline` when the posting run reviews it itself. Absent means the daemon chains a reviewer, which is what every handoff meant before SC-5476.

events.name: implementation-failed
events.where: board_failure.go — guarded by stageAlreadyFailed (SC-3857): a stage already failed with no relaunch since does not re-post, but the automatic in-place relaunch still runs (deps.Retry.tryRelaunch reads the stage's own recorded exit, not the marker thread)
events.doc: The daemon's failure watcher classifies an agent that exited without posting its handoff. It fires for the implementation stage as a whole — failedTypeFor(BoardImplementation) knows the stage, never which phase the run had reached — so every state of the stage leads here. Fires at most once per ending: a second exit event for the same dead run is absorbed (SC-3857).

events.name: start-review
events.where: board_failure.go chainReviewAfterCleanBuild; board_reconcile.go if that hook was lost
events.doc: Automatic: a clean build whose handoff names a reachable branch flows straight into its review. A handoff carrying `review: inline` is NOT chained here — the run that posted it is already reviewing it (start-inline-review) — unless the container that posted it is gone, which makes the handoff an orphan and this edge its recovery. The previous wording claimed the daemon simply never launches a second reviewer for a board fix run; it did, one second after the handoff, because nothing on the ticket said otherwise until SC-5476 put it there.

events.name: start-inline-review
events.doc: A board fix run reviews its own work in the same warm container: the handoff and this marker come from the same process, seconds apart. It is a real edge out of handed-off and had no row here until SC-5476, which is why nothing caught that the daemon took start-review in the gap between the two. This launcher posts no [human:claim], so claimWon cannot arbitrate it against the daemon's; what keeps the stage single-owner is the `review: inline` line on the handoff, which the daemon's launchers read before deciding to chain.

events.name: review-verdict
events.doc: Pass and fail are the same marker and the same state — the verdict rides in a field. Whether that verdict BLOCKS is decided once, by daemon.VerdictFailed, and shipped to the board as verdictFailed; the board never re-tests the string. A blocking verdict keeps the item out of Deploy and offers the rework gesture instead. The optional commits field records WHICH commits the verdict judged, so a later handoff can be compared against the work rather than the clock (SC-5475). In the inline topology the poster is the implementation container itself, which then posts its `[human:fix-summary]` and ENDS: the run's own last act is that summary, markers posted by later stages are not its business, and it never adds a plain comment (the shared run-end rule, SC-5691).

events.name: review-failed
events.doc: The review stage itself failed — a binding gate such as a missing branch or unreachable commits — not a failing verdict.
events.where: internal/daemon/board_failure.go — the failure watcher, via failedTypeFor(BoardVerification), guarded by stageAlreadyFailed (SC-3857): a stage already failed with no relaunch since does not re-post, but the automatic in-place relaunch still runs (deps.Retry.tryRelaunch reads the stage's own recorded exit, not the marker thread)

events.name: start-deploy
events.where: cmd/cmddeploy/deploy.go RunDeploy → internal/daemon/deploy_entry.go StartDeploy — the shared pre-deploy entry that refuses on an open decision, refuses on a blocking verification verdict (daemon.VerdictFailed, read through the card so a later handoff retires it), records the start, and then enters the review loop (reviewThenShip) instead of running the engine directly
events.guard: no board-<key>-implementation or board-<key>-verification container is alive in the checkout — waited for, up to DeployCheckoutWaitBound (deploy-launch-deferred)
events.doc: `human deploy KEY`. The one edge into deploying that a person takes, and it is taken by a command rather than by hand — posting the marker yourself posts it twice, which is why this edge carries its own command. The wide src is the honest list of where a CLI deploy starts from: a card whose handoff names the branch (handed-off, reviewed), a card whose deploy already failed (stopped, substrate-down), and a card with --branch given explicitly and no pipeline history at all (filed, ticket-reviewed, planned) — the 15 Backlog-to-Done histories in the replay corpus. The board's Deploy drop does NOT walk this edge — it fronts the merge with the PR review loop and records pr-review-started (start-pr-review); pre-loop board histories that carry deploy-started walked it before SC-1387. A card in awaiting-decision walks the separate start-deploy-override edge below, not this one — its command differs and offering this one's plain `human deploy <KEY>` there would be advertising a command the runtime refuses. Since F10 the edge no longer runs the engine on its own: the entry pushes the branch, opens its pull request in draft and launches the machine reviewer, so the item continues along pr-opened exactly as a board deploy does, and the merge is the loop's (pr-review-passed → ci-gate → merged). Two things short-circuit that: an approval the loop already recorded for exactly this head (approval-reused), and the person's --ready (deploy-skips-review). From reviewed the edge is taken only while the verdict does not block; a blocking verdict is refused before any push, with no marker, because the ticket already says what has to happen. A process with no launcher — the bare CLI with no daemon — cannot run the review and refuses without --ready rather than merging on CI alone; forwarded to the daemon, the command borrows the daemon's own engine wiring (Server.TransitionDeps). A host whose launch gate refuses the reviewer is refused here too, before the marker and the push, with no marker posted — the condition belongs to the machine, not the ticket. The checkout interlock fronts this edge from every one of its sources, and `--ready` does not lift it: that flag overrides the machine review, and the engine it runs writes to the same tree (SC-5691).

events.name: start-deploy-override
events.where: cmd/cmddeploy/deploy.go RunDeploy → internal/daemon/deploy_entry.go StartDeploy — the shared pre-deploy entry that refuses on an open decision and records the start before the engine (DeployBranch) runs
events.doc: Split from start-deploy so the way-out an asker in awaiting-decision is handed actually runs: `human deploy <KEY>` alone is refused from this state (deploy_entry.go StartDeploy), so the command this edge advertises carries the flag. awaiting-decision is a source ONLY under this flag — the refusal is the default, and overriding it is a person deciding to ship past their own open question, never an agent's default path.

events.name: pr-opened
events.doc: The pull request is opened as a draft, so a half-reviewed change is not mergeable by anyone. This is the `human deploy` route's entry into the loop (F10): the board's Deploy drop records pr-review-started without passing through deploying (start-pr-review), so this edge is walked only by a deploy that started from the CLI — the fix skills' `human deploy <KEY> --branch`, and a person's hand-run ship. The start marker's `branch:` is the loop's own binding: the merge step, the fixer dispatch and the approval marker all read the branch from it, falling back to the handoff only when it carries none — a loop started from the CLI has no handoff, and reading the handoff alone pushed an empty branch on approval (SC-5119). Every reviewer launch goes through launchPRReview, which first merges an advanced base into the local branch (Deployer.FreshenBranch) so the reviewer reads the integrated candidate; a conflict on that merge, or a clean merge that leaves the project's fast test tier red, walks stale-base-conflict instead (SC-5279). The local branch it merges into is reconciled with origin first: a ref this machine holds that carries nothing origin lacks is moved to origin's tip before the merge, so a branch a person repaired on the forge is read as it now is rather than as a ghost that re-finds an already-fixed conflict (SC-5596).
events.where: internal/daemon/deploy_entry.go StartDeploy → reviewThenShip, which opens the draft (openDraftPR, shared with the board's runDoneStage) and launches the reviewer through launchPRReview → launchPRLoopAgent

events.name: approval-reused
events.guard: a [human:pr-review-passed] newer than any later pr-review-started or ready-for-review names this branch and a head, and the pull request's head is that head
events.where: internal/daemon/deploy_entry.go StartDeploy → reviewThenShip → approvalCoversPR / currentApproval
events.doc: A re-run `human deploy` on work the loop already approved — a deploy that failed at its CI gate and is being re-driven by hand — does not spend a review round on a head the reviewer already judged: the draft is un-drafted on the strength of the bound approval and the engine runs the CI gate and merge. The binding is the whole of the rule: ticket, branch and head must all match, and the forge must report the head. A start marker, a non-draft pull request, or a passing verification verdict is not approval, and approval of an older revision does not authorise changed work (SC-3852 shipped with none of this and SC-4406 reached main unreviewed).

events.name: deploy-skips-review
events.where: internal/daemon/deploy_entry.go StartDeploy — MergeDraftPR runs the engine directly; settleDraft un-drafts a PR the loop is holding
events.doc: The person's override of the review interlock. `--ready` used to mean only 'un-draft the PR the loop is holding' (SC-4027); since F10 it also means 'do not start the machine review', because without it the CLI route always does. It is a person judging the change reviewed enough, never an agent's default path — the fix skills are told not to pass it — and the start marker records it as an override so the ticket never reads as a reviewed merge. It needs no launcher, which is what makes the bare CLI with no daemon still able to ship by hand.

events.name: pr-changes-requested
events.guard: bounded: the same class of blocking finding in the same file twice (SC-5278; identity fingerprint or class+file, whichever repeats), or DefaultPRReviewRounds (8) rounds — except a review that immediately follows a fix dispatch a done-stage outage interrupted, whose comparison is skipped for that one round (reviewFollowsOutagedFix, SC-5627)
events.doc: The fixer commits to the LOCAL branch and never pushes, so the reviewer reads the new commit rather than a stale pushed head. The pr-fix-started marker carries `finding:`, the fingerprint of the blocking finding the fixer was sent, which is what the next round compares against (SC-5174). It also carries `class:`, the file and the reviewer's category for that finding; the next round compares both, so the same class in the same file under a fresh slug is the same finding again (SC-5278). That comparison is skipped once when the fixer this pr-fix-started marker names never ran — a done-stage outage parked the card mid-fix and the uncharged re-drive re-entered straight at review, so the finding the reviewer is about to report again is the one the fixer was sent, not one it addressed and failed to fix (reviewFollowsOutagedFix, SC-5627); the skip is armed by this dispatch and disarmed only by the next one, so a re-drive that is itself outaged does not read as a second disagreement. The round's blocking findings are written to the durable findings record in the recall index (review_findings) by the loop driver (cmd/cmddaemon/prloopstate.go recordReviewRound), and the fixer's exit is attached to them when it reports.
events.where: internal/daemon/board_transition.go AdvancePRLoop, PRActionFix

events.name: pr-refixed
events.where: internal/daemon/board_transition.go AdvancePRLoop, PRActionReview → launchPRReview — the same action, re-entered after a fix round
events.doc: The reviewer re-reads the branch after the fixer's commit. It is the same review step rather than a different one, so what bounds the loop is the round count, not a separate escalating transition. The base merge in launchPRReview runs before every round, so a base that advanced during the fix round is folded in here rather than found by the reviewer as "branch behind main" (SC-5279).

events.name: pr-review-passed
events.where: board_transition.go AdvancePRLoop
events.doc: The reviewer approved. The draft is un-drafted and the item goes to the CI gate. This is the approval route, and it is not the only way in: the deploy gate itself now refuses a pull request it finds still in draft, before the CI wait rather than at the merge, and says the review loop is holding it — a person who has judged it reviewed enough overrides that with `human deploy --ready`, which un-drafts and ships (SC-4027). No automatic path clears the interlock, because a machine that can clear its own interlock has none. Recorded as a marker like every other outcome of the loop — success used to be the only transition here that left no trace, so a reader could not tell an approved review whose merge is running from a review still in flight. It also retires the loop sub-phase, so the badge stops reading 'PR review…' through the CI gate, rebase and merge. The marker binds what was approved: `branch:` and `head:`, the head the reviewer actually read (the fixer's local tip under the local-ref review model). A later `human deploy` reuses the approval only when it is still the newest word on the review — no later round, no later handoff — and the forge reports that exact head on the pull request (approval-reused); a marker with no head, posted before this field existed, is reusable by nothing. The loop has two drivers — the reviewer's Stop on the live hook path and reconcilePRLoops on its timer — and this marker is what tells the second one to stand down, but it is posted only after the first has decided, so the two can read the same approval before either has written. AdvancePRLoop therefore holds an in-process drive per ticket (prLoopDrives): a drive for a ticket already being driven does nothing, and the pass's next tick reads a thread the first drive has finished writing. A branch already on the base is recorded as merged here rather than as a failure to un-draft it, because the forge refuses to un-draft a merged pull request and that refusal is not a deploy failure (SC-5089).

events.name: pr-loop-escalates
events.doc: Budget spent, unreviewable, an outcome it cannot parse, or a fixer that stopped for a decision without naming one. That last case used to be raised as a question instead, assembled out of placeholders; a step that reports it is stuck and names neither the question nor a way forward has failed, and the reason carries the fixer's own summary so the card says what actually happened (SC-3630). It never merges on a state it cannot read. What does NOT fire it: a substrate failure mid-run. The hook reports a model API error as StopFailure and Claude Code retries through it, so the run carries on — driving the loop there read a verdict the reviewer had not written yet and reddened a review that went on to approve (SC-4026). Such an event is consumed and ignored; a run that genuinely dies on one is recovered by the durable re-drive, on the machine that owns the stage. Nor does a RECORDED outage: a reviewer or fixer that reports exit "outage" walks substrate-unreachable instead, uncharged (SC-5627). Nor does a review that follows a fix dispatch a done-stage outage interrupted before the fixer ran: the outaged re-drive re-enters straight at review, so the finding it is about to report again is the one the fixer was SENT, not one it addressed and failed to fix — reviewFollowsOutagedFix suppresses the repeat check for exactly that one round, armed by the fix dispatch and disarmed only by the next one, so a re-drive that is itself outaged does not read as a second disagreement (SC-5627). It also fires at most once per dead round: one run can raise both a StopFailure and a Stop, and an escalation with nothing changed since the last one is not restated. A re-drive from reconcilePRLoops carries no exit event and a snapshot older than the pass; when the thread it re-reads names a step with no record, it asks whether that step's agent is alive on this machine before escalating, and stands down if it is — the fixer launched by the hook path seconds earlier is work in progress, not a step the loop cannot read (SC-5120). What bounds the loop is repetition, not count (SC-5174): the reviewer's blocking finding being the one the fixer was already sent — by identity, or by class in the same file (SC-5278) — is the reviewer and fixer disagreeing, and the loop stops there naming the finding, or the file and class when that is what repeated; a round that finds a different problem is progress and continues, under DefaultPRReviewRounds (8) as the outer cap — the first four tickets through the machine review found a new real problem every round, and a cap of three turned five of those rounds into a person's turn.
events.where: internal/daemon/board_transition.go AdvancePRLoop — prEscalationReason names which of the three it was

events.name: ci-red
events.guard: bounded: 2 rounds, plus one per [human:deploy-retry] grant
events.doc: A red-but-mechanical failure dispatches the fixer instead of failing the item. A cancelled check counts as no answer yet, not as a no. Only a red a code change could turn green reaches here — a head red only on checks no code change could turn green never does. The dispatch carries the code-fixable failing checks and only those: a mixed head — a red build beside a red signature job — still dispatches, with the signature job left off the marker, because a fixer told to fix it looks for a defect that is not in the branch. A head red only on checks no code change could turn green takes deploy-failed instead, after DeployExternalCheckGrace (SC-5843). That stop, too, waits for every OTHER check to conclude first: a still-pending build or test beside an already-red signature check is not yet a verdict (SC-5843 r1).
events.where: internal/daemon/board_transition.go deployFailedOrDispatchFixer — ciFailureFixable decides fixer or stop, on the classification internal/daemon/deploy_checks.go stamps on the error (redHeadVerdict / checkIsExternal / deployExternalChecksDetail)

events.name: ci-regated
events.where: internal/daemon/board_transition.go AdvanceDeployFix — publishes the fixer's branch, then re-enters DeployBranch; a deploy-fix-started marker carrying `before: review` walks resolved-before-review instead
events.doc: The fixer's container holds no push credentials, so its deliverable is the local branch and the daemon publishes it before re-entering the gate. Publishing first is what makes the resolution count at all: the gate reads the branch from origin, so an unpublished fix would be silently discarded and the same failure re-hit. Publishing is not overwriting: the daemon publishes the resolution only while it is the side carrying the newer work, adopts origin's tip when origin carries work the resolution does not, and refuses — naming both heads — when each side carries changes the other lacks (SC-5596).

events.name: stale-base-conflict
events.guard: bounded: 2 rounds, shared with ci-red, plus one per [human:deploy-retry] grant
events.where: internal/daemon/board_transition.go launchPRReview → deployFailedOrDispatchFixer with beforeReview — every reviewer launch site (reviewThenShip, openDraftPRAndReview, AdvancePRLoop PRActionReview, AdvanceDeployFix done) passes through it
events.doc: The base advanced past the branch and merging it in conflicts, OR the merge is textually clean but the project's fast test tier fails on the merged result (a symbol renamed on the base against a new call site on the branch, the commonest form of this drift — acceptance criterion 1). Either way the fix is mechanical, so the deploy fixer takes it BEFORE any reviewer runs: run 3 of the campaign spent a review round on "branch behind main" on four of six pull requests, with the reviewer finding the drift, the fixer merging the base and the reviewer reading everything again. The marker's `before: review` field is what tells the fixer's done exit to hand back to the reviewer rather than re-run the deploy. A clean merge that also passes the fast tier posts nothing: the local ref moves to the merge commit and the reviewer launch proceeds on the source edge. `reviewed` and `stopped` cover openDraftPRAndReview (runDoneStage's board-Deploy-drop route, which calls launchPRReview before any pr-review-started marker is posted, so the item is still sitting where start-pr-review found it); `deploy-fixing` covers AdvanceDeployFix's own before-review handback (resolved-before-review) hitting a second conflict on the base it re-merges — the item has not yet reached pr-review when that second freshen runs (SC-5279).

events.name: resolved-before-review
events.where: internal/daemon/board_transition.go AdvanceDeployFix — deployFixWasBeforeReview reads the newest deploy-fix-started marker; the fixer's branch is published first, then launchPRReview runs
events.doc: The fixer resolved a pre-review base conflict; nothing has reviewed the integrated branch yet, so the review is what comes next, not the CI gate. launchPRReview merges the base again on the way in — a base that moved during the fix round is folded in, and a second conflict spends a second fixer round from the same bound (SC-5279).

events.name: ci-green-merged
events.doc: If the base moved on, the branch is rebased and CI re-gated on the new head before merging. Past the merge, branch cleanup and closing the ticket are best-effort and never fail the item. A branch already merged into the base is the same outcome reached without a PR at all: the engine records it and stops, which is why the merge is reachable directly from deploying. A merge the forge refuses because the head is out of date (409) is not a failure: it means the base moved under the gate, usually a sibling deploy landing seconds earlier. The forge's own lag clears inside the merge-retry window; a refusal that outlives it re-runs the freshness stage, re-gates CI on the head it publishes and merges, bounded by DeployMergeReintegrations.
events.where: internal/daemon/board_transition.go DeployBranch — one engine, entered from the board and from `human deploy` (cmd/cmddeploy/deploy.go RunDeploy)

events.name: shipped-after-stop
events.doc: A merge recorded onto a card that had already been declared failed. Three producers reach it as described by this edge: a deploy fixer that converged AFTER a spurious [human:deploy-failed] was posted over its still-running fixer, whose done exit calls the engine directly with no marker in between; reconcileShippedFailures retiring a stale red whose pull request the forge reports merged; and a board Deploy re-drop whose branch is already on the base, which short-circuits to the same terminal success path. The marker says HOW the work shipped — `pr` on the ordinary path, `merged` for a branch already in the base — so this edge fixes neither field. Until SC-5594 the machine had no edge here while the stopped state's own prose and four corpus histories (SC-3339, SC-3346, SC-3497, SC-3508) all showed the sequence, so the strict local tracker refused the only record the merge had and the engine, which discarded the refusal and closed the ticket anyway, left a ticket Done over a failed-deploy trail. `stopped` is the ticket's one shared failure state — planning-failed, fix-budget-spent, implementation-failed, review-failed, pr-loop-escalates, launch-refused-no-plan, plan-redrive-exhausted, stage-relaunch-refused and legacy-pr-failed all have dst `stopped` — so this src (`["stopped"]`) admits `deployed` after ANY of those, not only after a deploy-stage failure; the replay corpus shows it firing on cards stopped by launch-refused-no-plan/plan-redrive-exhausted (SC-2804) and by pr-loop-escalates (SC-2989), neither of which ran a deploy at all. That breadth is not the `human deploy --branch` bypass SC-3852 closed: that shape never enters the machine — it posts `deployed` directly onto filed, planned or awaiting-decision with no prior stage marker — and is still refused from those three states (see retired.deployed@stopped and violations.deployed@filed/planned/awaiting-decision in replay-baseline.json); what refuses it is SC-3852's own entry-point check, not a narrower version of this edge.
events.where: internal/daemon/board_transition.go DeployBranch (both the post-merge record and the already-merged carve-out) and openDraftPRAndReview's carve-out — each posts through recordDeployedBestEffort, which retries and warns rather than discarding the refusal, and closes the ticket only when the record landed; internal/daemon/board_reconcile.go reconcileShippedFailures posts the same marker for an out-of-band merge

events.name: deploy-failed
events.doc: The deploy gave up. The marker names the condition that is blocking — for a deploy-fixer escalation it quotes the failure the fixer was dispatched to fix, which for CI names the red checks — and it does not offer a gesture that cannot work: where re-running Deploy would hit the same failure, it says so instead of advising the retry. When the deploy fixer stopped needs-human-work, the marker also carries the fixer's blocker as the optional fields kind, evidence, attempted and release, copied from stage.deploy-fix (SC-5179). When automated deploy-fixer rounds preceded the failure, the reason states how many ran — the escalation arm (deployFixEscalationReason) and the budget-exhausted fallback (deployFailedOrDispatchFixer) both do — so 'no automation exists for this' and 'two rounds ran and gave up' are never the same sentence; a failure with no rounds behind it claims none (SC-3640). Where the fix budget is what is blocking — the rounds are spent and no grant stands — the reason also says so and names the gesture that lifts it, because the marker must not leave a person looking at a red card whose only offered move appears to be the one that just failed: 'The automated fix budget for this ticket is spent; Retry deploy on the card grants one further fix round.' Only the board's gesture is named, never `human deploy`, which grants nothing (SC-5595). What does NOT fire it from deploy-fixing: a substrate failure mid-run. The hook reports a model API error as StopFailure and Claude Code retries through it, so driveDeployFixExit consumes the event and withholds the worktree handoff rather than reading a report the fixer has not written — the guard drivePRLoopExit had since SC-4026 and this driver never did (SC-5627). One reason reaches here instead of the fixer even though the checks themselves reported it: a head red only on checks no code change can turn green. The marker names those checks and asks for a re-run of them, never a code fix (SC-5843).
events.where: internal/daemon/board_transition.go deployFailed (NOT guarded by stageAlreadyFailed — it can fire before any running done-stage marker exists at all, e.g. a push failure ahead of pr-review-started, so a guard there would swallow a genuine new failure on a board Deploy re-drop, SC-3857 AD5), and AdvanceDeployFix for a fixer that did not converge (guarded by stageAlreadyFailed: a dispatch that actually started a fixer posts deploy-fix-started first, so the guard cannot hide that dispatch's own failure; a dispatch REFUSED because a fixer is already running posts nothing and leaves the guard on, deliberately — see deploy-fixer-launch-refused, SC-4244)

events.name: stage-asks
events.where: board_state.go pauseOnOpenOptions
events.prompt: human-plan-skill.md, human-autofix-skill.md Step 1a/7.3, human-security-fix-skill.md Step 1a/7.3, human-review-skill.md, human-pickup-review-skill.md
events.doc: A stage found a genuine fork and stopped. The item is not working and not dead — it is waiting on a person, and reads as decision-needed rather than running. From in-review/fixing/implementing it is raised only for a reviewer Summary of `decision-required`, checked before any verdict is posted by every skill that dispatches human-reviewer (human-review-skill.md, human-pickup-review-skill.md, human-autofix-skill.md, human-security-fix-skill.md); a review that reaches pass/pass with notes/fail/incomplete posts that verdict and never also this marker for the same review (SC-5277).

events.name: decision-made
events.where: board_options.go ApplyOption → pursueDecision — records the choice, then starts the stage unless the answer was to wait; board_state.go optionChosenQueued reads the window between the two
events.doc: A human picked an answer. This records it and nothing more: pursueDecision posts the choice comment and only then calls startAgentStage, so the item is queued for a stage before it is running in one. ONE answer stops there: an option carrying a `waits-for-<id>` line means this ticket goes second, so the choice is recorded with that ticket named on it and no stage is started at all. Starting it is the exact opposite of what was chosen, and it was the machine's only move on any answer until an answer could say otherwise — nothing in an option's prose distinguishes "SC-1 goes first" from "do it this way". The stage that gets queued is the one the RECORD names — written onto the option-chosen marker itself, with the block read only for choices recorded before that field existed — not the one the item sits in — planning is the common case, while a PR-loop escalation deliberately names implementation even though the item is in the deploy stage, because the fixer raised a question only a code change can answer and the rebuild re-adopts the still-open draft PR. The item pauses correctly meanwhile, because an open block pauses every card whose own stage ranks at or after the one named. The stage is derived; the state is not — every answered decision lands here first. A wait that nothing could clear — on the ticket itself, or on a ticket already held on this one — is refused at ApplyOption (refuseWaitCycle) and the block stays open; a pair recorded before that guard is reported on both card faces by MarkWaitCycles and never released by waitCleared, since neither partner can close (SC-5274).

events.name: substrate-unreachable
events.where: board_retry.go ExitOutage for the four board stages; internal/daemon/board_transition.go AdvanceDeployFix → deployFixUnreachable → doneStageOutage for the deploy-fix step and AdvancePRLoop → prLoopOutage → doneStageOutage (PRActionOutage) for the two PR-loop steps — all three exits are claimed by their own driver (driveDeployFixExit / drivePRLoopExit) before the generic outage gate can see them (SC-5592, SC-5627)
events.doc: One marker per stage. It costs no retry budget and the reconcile pass relaunches it each interval until the substrate returns. The deploy-fix step reaches it only from deploy-fixing: the post sits under the stageAlreadyFailed guard, so a done stage another actor already redded stays red rather than flipping back to waiting. The round it spent is given back — deployFixRounds discards a deploy-fix-started marker that a deploy-outage marker follows — so a persisting outage cannot exhaust the 2-round budget on rounds that attempted nothing. The PR review→fix loop reaches it from pr-review and pr-fix, on the DONE stage's own marker: the loop has none of its own and needs none, because substrate-down is stage-agnostic and redeploy-after-outage is already the way back in. Both posts sit under the same guard as the deploy fixer's — a done stage another actor already redded stays red rather than flipping back to waiting — and for the loop that guard reads the derived state, because the done stage has two failed markers and the loop's own is [human:pr-review-failed]. The round is given back the same way: chargedPRReviewRounds and deployFixRounds share one walk (roundsNetOfOutage) that discards a started marker a deploy-outage marker follows, so a persisting outage can exhaust neither the 2-round fix budget nor DefaultPRReviewRounds on rounds that attempted nothing (SC-5627). Narrowed by SC-5840 for the deploy-fix step: an outage this daemon's own proxy explains — a host it refused by policy, recorded as a `block` event within EgressBlockWindow — does not walk this edge at all. It takes one of the egress-blocked-by-policy-* events to stopped instead, because the substrate in that case is a line missing from a config file on this host and no wait can restore it; deployFixUnreachable splits that case off before calling doneStageOutage.

events.name: egress-blocked-by-policy-planning
events.where: internal/daemon/board_egressblock.go postEgressBlockedFailure, reached from board_outage.go handleOutageExit and board_reconcile.go reconcileOutage (a card already parked in substrate-down); board_retry.go classifyRelaunch returns relaunchNone for the same fact, so neither the live exit path nor reconcileFailedStages nor reconcileOneStuckCard re-drives it
events.doc: The one ending that SAYS outage and is not one, for the planning stage. A host this daemon's own proxy refuses by policy is closed with no TLS alert, so inside the container it is byte-identical to a dead network and the agent honestly records exit: outage — and the uncharged outage re-drive then repeated a missing config line every reconcile tick for up to OutageWaitBound (six fixer containers in twelve minutes, SC-5840). The daemon held the block fact the whole time: its proxy emits a `block` event into the NetworkEventStore at the moment it refuses. Correlating the two within EgressBlockWindow reclassifies the stop: the stage's own *-failed marker, with the host and the exact proxy.domains line to add as the blocker's release condition, kind unavailable-dependency. It charges NOTHING and is said ONCE, under the same stageAlreadyFailed guard every other *-failed post takes. No relaunch follows: the release is a person editing .humanconfig.yaml and restarting the daemon. A model-boundary pause and an implausible refused host are deliberately NOT reclassified this way — see egress-blocked-by-policy-implementation's doc for the shared rationale, repeated once per stage-specific event so each carries its own precise src rather than one event spanning every stage's marker (a wide event pairing every src against every marker absorbed an unrelated corpus violation, implementation-failed@planning, SC-5840). Distinct from not_states / `a host that cannot launch`, which is the SAME condition caught BEFORE a stage starts (the egress doctor check, SC-4819): there no stage ran and no ticket is blamed, here a stage ran and reported what it saw.
events.prompt: shared/exit-contract.md and human-deploy-fixer-agent.md — the `outage` row names the one case the daemon overrides

events.name: egress-blocked-by-policy-implementation
events.where: internal/daemon/board_egressblock.go postEgressBlockedFailure, reached from board_outage.go handleOutageExit and board_reconcile.go reconcileOutage (a card already parked in substrate-down); board_retry.go classifyRelaunch returns relaunchNone for the same fact, so neither the live exit path nor reconcileFailedStages nor reconcileOneStuckCard re-drives it
events.doc: The one ending that SAYS outage and is not one, for the implementation stage — the incident's own route (SC-5840): six fixer containers in twelve minutes, each honestly reporting outage while `github.com` sat outside a wildcard-only allowlist. The daemon held the block fact the whole time: its proxy emits a `block` event into the NetworkEventStore the moment it refuses a host.
